title: Fundamentalism: Menace II Society
summary: Josh and Chuck open with tour and show shoutouts (Pavement in Boston, Bonnie 'Prince' Billy shows, Will Oldham), then examine fundamentalism as an ideology rather than only a theology. They trace its origins to the 1870s Fundamentals pamphlets and the Baptist and Presbyterian struggles, the 1859 Darwin challenge, the 1925 Scopes Monkey Trial and its underground period, the late-1970s second wave (Christian right, Moral Majority, Iranian Revolution, Hindu nationalism in India, Israel, Uganda). They discuss traits such as intolerance, reactivity to threats, simplistic answers, anti-science attitudes, conspiracy thinking, and charismatic authoritarian leaders, and debate American founding documents (Virginia Charter, Constitution's 'science' clause, Jefferson on church and state). They close with modernization, reasons people are drawn to fundamentalism, and ideas for responding to it, such as reading fiction, travel, and friendship. The episode ends with a listener mail about vasectomy experiences and a sign-off.

entities.name: On the Origin of the Species

segments.title: Opening banter and tour shoutouts
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck announce upcoming live shows, then chat about Pavement and Bonnie Prince Billy shows, Will Oldham, and breakfast burritos.

segments.title: Introduction: fundamentalism as ideology
segments.summary: The hosts introduce fundamentalism as an ideology that can arise around anything people hold dear, not only religion, and note that it is a modern movement starting around 1870.

segments.title: First wave: The Fundamentals and Darwin
segments.summary: The first wave began with The Fundamentals pamphlets as a response to religious progressivism. Darwin's 1859 book challenged creationism and helped spark the movement.

segments.title: Scopes Monkey Trial and going underground
segments.summary: The 1925 Tennessee trial of teacher John Scopes, with Clarence Darrow as his lawyer, exposed fundamentalist beliefs. Afterward the movement went underground and built its own institutions.

segments.title: Second wave: Christian right and global movements
segments.summary: In the late 1970s fundamentalism returned, with the Christian right entering politics through groups like the Moral Majority and Christian Coalition and figures like Pat Robertson. Similar movements appeared in Iran, Israel, India, and Africa.

segments.title: Coincidence of movements and the Christian right in politics
segments.summary: The hosts reflect on how these movements arose at about the same time, and how fundamentalism has blurred church and state in American politics.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Brief break before returning to the topic.

segments.title: Misconceptions and fundamentalism beyond religion
segments.summary: Fundamentalism is not only a religious problem. People can be fundamentalist about things like the Second Amendment, free markets, or constitutional originalism. Intolerance is a key marker, illustrated by the Amish.

segments.title: Traits of fundamentalism
segments.summary: Traits include reaction to perceived threats, simplistic answers, blind obedience, anti-science views, conspiracy thinking, and admiration for charismatic authoritarian leaders. Evangelical links to QAnon are discussed.

segments.title: American founding documents and modernization
segments.summary: Fundamentalists cite religious language in founding documents. The hosts respond with the Virginia Charter context, the Constitution's science clause, and Jefferson on church and state, and discuss modernization as the driver of fundamentalism.

segments.title: Why people join and ways to respond
segments.summary: People drawn to fundamentalism often feel left behind or uncertain. Suggested responses include reading fiction, travel, friendship, and reassuring alternatives, with debate over tolerance of intolerance.

segments.title: Listener mail: vasectomy experiences
segments.summary: A listener named Ryan describes his vasectomy recovery and corrects the hosts on the procedure, noting that a small section of the vas deferens is removed and sent for tissue sampling.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and invite listener mail.
